To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a thioredoxinnucleoside dphosphate kinase (TXNDC3) is involved in PCD (a genetic condition characterized by respiratory tract infections, situs inversus, and infertility).

the combination of a nonsense mutation and an intronic SNP in the TXNDC3 gene results in the generation of two isoforms of TXNDC-3, a thioredoxinnucleoside dphosphate kinase, with a reduced amount of the isoform lacking exon 7, and the resulting imbalance of the two isoforms leads to a defect of the microtubule network of the cilia and to primary ciliary dyskiniesia.

a nonsense mutation in TXNDC3 combined with a common intronic SNP causes primary ciliary dykinesia, a genetic condition characterized, among other things, by chronic respiratory infections, male infertility and randomization of left-right asymmetry.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a new gene implicated in PCD and the characterization of the molecular mechanism underlying a rare Mendelian condition.
the identification of new genes and molecular mechanisms underlying a human disease.
the discovery of a new molecular mechanism underlying PCD and a new role for thioredoxins in human disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TXNDC3 is a novel gene for PCD.
the disease results from the combination of a nonsense mutation and an intronic SNP, which affects the ratio of the two physiological TXNCD3 isoforms, the longer one being the most abundant.
TXNDC3 is a novel gene involved in PCD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a nonsense mutation combined with a common variant in a thioredoxine-nucleoside triphosphate kinase gene, TXNDC2, is the cause of PCD.
the combination of two genetic defects, which are common in human populations, can lead to a severe genetic disorder.
we identified a gene involved in PCD and that this gene is a member of the TXN family of proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the study of rare diseases can be a fruitful way to identify new genes involved in human physiology.
the study of rare diseases can uncover novel genes and pathways that are relevant to more common disorders.
the identification of the molecular basis of PCD has been extended to a novel class of proteins, the thioredoxins.
